newsitem.title: INDIA: Motley Indian coalition confronts budget test.
newsitem.headline: Motley Indian coalition confronts budget test.

text.p: The Indian government presents a new budget plan on Friday that analysts said will test the cohesion of the 15-party coalition government and New Delhi's commitment to open-market reforms.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was set to unveil the spending and tax plan for the next fiscal year to the lower house of parliament at 5 p.m. (1130 GMT).

India began jettisoning more than four decades of socialist controls in 1991 when, faced with a foreign exchange crisis, it started gradually opening up to foreign investment and trade, and dismantling state controls.

But the government retains considerable clout, and the annual budget, in this case for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1, sets a sweeping agenda affecting interests ranging from teeming rural poor to rich foreign investors.

Chidambaram's budget, his first full-fledged blueprint since Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda took office last June following inconclusive general elections, has major implications for the centre-left coalition, made up of free traders to communists.
"Given the competing interests, he has very little room for manoeuvre," a Finance Ministry official said.

A bespectacled, Harvard-educated economic liberal, Chidambaram must also walk a tightrope between the twin demands of restraining the fiscal deficit and spurring sluggish industrial growth, while keeping a sympathetic eye on the poor.

The political equation is doubly delicate as, in addition to critics in the left wing of the coalition, Chidambaram faces a cool Congress party and a right-wing Hindu opposition ready to pounce on any divisions in the government.
"Pity Mr Chidambaram," read a headline in the Observer newspaper.
The Bombay Stock Exchange staged a pre-budget rally on Friday. The bourse's benchmark index was up 62.81 points, or 1.83 percent, to 3,490.68 at 1:15 p.m. (0745 GMT).
A survey by the Economic Times showed 55 percent of the executives polled expected the budget to be favourable to business.

The investment community is expecting Chidambaram to reiterate the government's commitment to budgetary restraint. The fiscal deficit, which stood at 5.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) one year ago, is anticipated to fall to between 5.1 and 5.4 percent of GDP by the end of March.
Chidambaram is expected to announce a deficit target of about 4.5 percent of GDP for 1997/98.

To bring in more revenues, he may announce an ambitious programme to sell off partial stakes in state-controlled firms. The government fell well short of its disinvestment targets over the past two years because of lacklustre capital markets.
The finance minister is expected to cast a wider tax net, probably slapping new levies on luxury items such as cars and high-cost hotels.

To spur industrial growth, which slowed to 9.8 percent between April and December 1996 from 11.7 percent in the same period in 1995, the government is expected to try to lure more private investment into core industries such as power and telecommunications, where bottlenecks are hampering output.
For markets, Chidambaram was said to be considering allowing firms to buy back their own shares, removing a corporate tax surcharge and scrapping double taxation of dividends.
But a controversial 12.9 percent minimum alternate tax (MAT) on companies may be retained, although analysts said Chidambaram might tinker with depreciation rates to ease the MAT's impact.
